name: Naimisharanya
event: Framing recital of the entire Mahabharata to Shaunaka and the assembled sages
description:
Naimisharanya holds a uniquely sacred threshold in Sanskrit epic literature as the setting for the frame narrative of the Mahabharata. Situated along the banks of the Gomati River, this ancient forested hermitage was described as an inviolable sanctuary where time slows and profound philosophical discourses unfold away from the turbulence of royal courts.

Here, during a twelve-year sacrificial conclave presided over by the kulapati Shaunaka, the bard Ugrasrava Sauti—son of Lomaharshana—arrived after attending the catastrophic snake sacrifice (Sarpa Satra) of King Janamejaya at Takshashila. At the earnest request of the assembled rishis, Sauti began chanting the comprehensive version of the great epic originally conceived by Krishna Dvaipayana Vyasa and recited by his disciple Vaishampayana.

Modern Nimsar in the Sitapur district of Uttar Pradesh remains an enduring centre of pilgrimage, centered on the ancient Chakra Tirtha—a circular water basin believed by tradition to mark where the wheel of Dharma struck the earth.
imageCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Archaeological Survey of India

name: Hastinapura
event: Imperial seat of the Kuru dynasty; venue of the tragic dicing match and assembly of elders
description:
Hastinapura, named after King Hastin of the lunar dynasty, stood as the majestic imperial metropolis of the Kurus on the right bank of the Ganga. It formed the political epicentre of the epic, witnessing the early upbringing of the hundred Kaurava princes and their five Pandava cousins under the strict tutelage of Bhishma, Dronacharya, and Kripacharya.

The royal sabha at Hastinapura became the crucible of dynastic downfall. In the ill-famed gambling pavilion constructed on Dhritarashtra's command, Shakuni exploited Yudhishthira's compliance in the dice match, leading inexorably to the disrobing of Draupadi before silent patriarchs and the bitter decree of twelve years in exile followed by a year in concealment.

Excavations directed by archaeologist B.B. Lal between 1950 and 1952 at the mound of Hastinapur revealed a sequence of Painted Grey Ware (PGW) occupational strata datable to the early 1st millennium BCE. Remarkably, the layer corresponding to Period II showed evidence of heavy erosion caused by severe flooding of the Ganga, directly corroborating the Puranic record of King Nicakshu shifting the Kuru capital downstream to Kaushambi.
imageCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Archaeological Survey of India

name: Varanavata
event: The plot of the lac palace (Lakshagraha) and subterranean escape of the Pandavas
description:
Varanavata was an ancient settlement situated along the confluence of the Hindon and Krishna rivers. In the Adi Parva, Prince Duryodhana, consumed by jealousy over Yudhishthira's popular acclaim as heir apparent, convinced his blind father Dhritarashtra to send Kunti and the five Pandavas to Varanavata on the pretext of attending a festival celebrating Lord Pashupati.

Under royal instruction, the artisan Purochana erected a lavish palace engineered entirely with combustible materials—hemp, lac, resin, clarified butter, and dried grass. Having received a coded mleccha-dialect warning from the wise councillor Vidura before departure, the Pandavas engaged a trusted royal miner to excavate an underground tunnel running from the inner chamber to the safety of the riverbank. On a pitch-dark night, Bhima set fire to the mansion, leaving Purochana trapped inside while the Pandavas escaped secretly into the wilderness.

Modern Barnawa in Uttar Pradesh features a prominent ancient mound traditionally designated as the Lakshagraha mound. Trial trenching has yielded characteristic Painted Grey Ware sherds, reinforcing the site's antiquity, though scholarly consensus distinguishes the archaeological antiquity of the settlement from the literal literary narrative.

name: Ekachakra
modernLocation: Erach / Betwa Valley, Jhansi district, Uttar Pradesh (alternatively Birbhum, Bengal)
event: Disguised dwelling of the Pandavas as mendicants; slaying of the demon Bakasura by Bhima
description:
Following their flight from the burning mansion at Varanavata, the Pandavas crossed multiple rivers under cover of darkness and assumed the garb of itinerant Brahmins. Guided by the sage Vyasa, they sought shelter in the quiet provincial town of Ekachakra, staying in the home of an hospitable Brahmin family and sustaining themselves on daily alms.

The town lived under the reign of terror of Bakasura, a predatory cannibalistic Asura residing in an adjacent cavern. In exchange for not devastating the whole town, Bakasura demanded a weekly tribute comprising a cartload of rice, two buffaloes, and the unfortunate person delivering the meal. Hearing the wailing of their host family whose turn had arrived, Kunti intervened and sent the formidable Bhima in their stead. At the demon's lair, Bhima calmly consumed the demon's food before engaging Bakasura in a ferocious wrestling match, ultimately snapping the demon's spine across his knee and freeing the populace.

The geographic identification of Ekachakra remains disputed among historians and local folklore. While prominent regional traditions claim sites such as Kaivara in Karnataka or Ekachakra/Khadigram in Birbhum (West Bengal), classical Indologists place the epic journey within the northern Yamuna-Betwa corridor, frequently identifying it with ancient Erach on the Betwa River.

name: Kampilya
event: Swayamvara of Princess Draupadi; Arjuna pierces the revolving fish target
description:
Kampilya was the fortified southern capital of the Panchala kingdom, ruled by King Drupada along the fertile banks of the Ganges. Renowned as a center of philosophy and statecraft, it served as the rival kingdom balancing Kuru hegemony in northern Aryavarta.

In Kampilya's royal amphitheatre, Drupada convened the swayamvara of his fire-born daughter Krishnaa (Draupadi), setting a test of martial prowess that no ordinary prince could accomplish: stringing an immense composite bow and shooting five arrows through a whirling gold target into the eye of an overhead fish while looking only at its reflection in oil. While famed kings and warriors failed in ignominy, Arjuna—still disguised as an impoverished Brahmin ascetic—stepped into the arena, strung the mighty weapon with effortless grace, and hit the target, winning the princess's garland.

Archaeological excavations at the Drupad Qila mound in modern Kampil have exposed substantial cultural strata including Painted Grey Ware (PGW) and Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW), placing Kampilya among the best-documented early iron age urban centres of the middle Ganga valley.
imageCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Archaeological Survey of India

name: Indraprastha
event: Founding of the Pandava capital; construction of Maya Sabha and Rajasuya sacrifice
description:
When the Kuru kingdom was partitioned to avoid civil war, the Pandavas were granted Khandavaprastha—a wild, desolate woodland bordering the Yamuna. With the celestial architect Maya Danava, whom Arjuna and Krishna spared during the burning of the Khandava forest, the princes cleared the land and raised Indraprastha, a radiant capital conceived as an earthly counterpart to the heavenly city of Indra.

At its heart stood the legendary Maya Sabha, an assembly hall engineered with optical marvels, reflecting pools mistaken for polished crystal floors, and solid marble surfaces resembling clear water. It was in this hall that Yudhishthira performed the imperial Rajasuya sacrifice, establishing his suzerainty over the known world. The hall also witnessed Duryodhana's public humiliation when he stepped into water he presumed was stone, an incident that hardened his resolve to destroy the Pandavas.

Tradition firmly identifies Indraprastha with the high mound of Purana Qila in central New Delhi. Systematic excavations conducted by the Archaeological Survey of India under B.B. Lal and subsequent directors uncovered stratified deposits beginning with Painted Grey Ware (c. 1000–600 BCE), followed by continuous Northern Black Polished Ware, Shunga, Kushan, and medieval occupations.
imageCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Archaeological Survey of India

name: Gandhara
modernLocation: Taxila & Peshawar Valley, Punjab / Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
event: Ancestral realm of Queen Gandhari and Prince Shakuni; northwestern frontier of the epic world
description:
Gandhara encompassed the rugged, fertile valleys of the Kabul and lower Indus rivers, serving as the northwestern gateway between the Indian subcontinent and central Eurasia. Governed by King Subala, the region was famed in epic geography for its spirited war horses, hardy hill fighters, and seasoned traders.

From Gandhara came two of the epic's most consequential figures: Queen Gandhari, who chose to blindfold herself for life out of devotion to her sightless husband Dhritarashtra, and her cunning brother Shakuni. Operating from Hastinapura, Shakuni brought Gandhara's sophisticated understanding of psychological statecraft and deceptive dice play to dismantle Pandava sovereignty from within.

The historical region of Gandhara is anchored archaeologically by monumental urban ruins at Pushkalavati (modern Charsadda) and Takshashila (Taxila). Both cities showcase deep strata from the 1st millennium BCE onwards and are designated UNESCO World Heritage sites, representing the cultural synthesis between early Vedic, Achaemenid, and Hellenistic traditions.

name: Mathura
event: Capital of the Shurasenas; birthplace of Krishna and overthrow of the tyrant Kamsa
description:
Mathura, situated strategically on the right bank of the Yamuna River, was the capital of the Shurasena kingdom and the cradle of the Vrishni and Andhaka confederacies. Throughout the epic era, Mathura stood at the crossroads of northern trade routes (Uttarapatha) connecting the Gangetic plains to the western seaboard.

It was here that Krishna and his elder brother Balarama were born into royal captivity, smuggled to Gokula across the flooding Yamuna, and returned as youths to overthrow their tyrannical maternal uncle Kamsa in his own wrestling arena. Although Kamsa was slain and King Ugrasena restored to the throne, continuous retaliatory sieges launched by Jarasandha, the formidable emperor of Magadha, ultimately compelled the Yadava leaders to migrate westward to the Gujarat coast.

Mathura is one of India's most extensively investigated archaeological landscapes. Excavations have revealed settlements dating to the Painted Grey Ware period (Period I, c. 1000 BCE) followed by a flourishing urban metropolis under the Mauryans, Shungas, and Kushans, yielding distinctive red sandstone sculptures that define early classical Indian art.

name: Kamyaka Forest
modernLocation: Western Haryana / Saraswati River basin, near Sirsa and Hisar
event: First forest retreat of the Pandavas during their twelve-year exile; visits by Krishna and Markandeya
description:
The Kamyaka Forest was a dense wilderness located on the western frontier of Kurukshetra, along the banks of the sacred Saraswati River where it meandered towards the Thar desert. Upon losing the rigged game of dice and departing Hastinapura, the Pandavas accompanied by loyal citizens and learned Brahmins made Kamyaka their first sustained retreat.

At the entry of Kamyaka, Bhima vanquished the man-eating Rakshasa Kirmira, brother of Bakasura, establishing safe passage for the exiled royals. Here, Krishna visited his cousins to offer solace and counsel, and revered sages including Markandeya and Brihadashva recounted timeless moral parables, including the stories of Nala-Damayanti and Savitri-Satyavan, to sustain the spirits of the disinherited princes.

As a geographical entity, Kamyaka represented the transitional woodland ecotone between the fertile Gangetic plain and the arid margins of western India. While specific settlement remains cannot be attributed to an ancient nomadic forest, literary descriptions consistently orient it along the dried paleochannels of the Saraswati system around modern Sirsa and Hisar in Haryana.

name: Dwarka
event: Island citadel of the Vrishnis founded by Krishna; submerged into the ocean after the departure of the Yadavas
description:
Dwarka (Dvaravati), known poeticallly as the 'City of Many Gates', was engineered as an impregnable maritime bastion on the westernmost promontory of the Kathiawar peninsula. Following sustained attacks on Mathura by Jarasandha of Magadha, Krishna led the Yadava clans across the desert to construct this prosperous harbour city, protected by sea channels and fortified stone ramparts.

Dwarka flourished as a cosmopolitan maritime kingdom, conducting oceanic trade and serving as Krishna's royal capital throughout the events of the Mahabharata. Thirty-six years after the Great War, following the fratricidal conflict at Prabhasa, Krishna departed the mortal world. As narrated in the Mausala Parva, Arjuna arrived to evacuate the surviving women, children, and elderly before the rising Arabian Sea surged ashore, submerging the palatial city beneath its waves.

Pioneering marine archaeological excavations directed by Dr. S.R. Rao of the National Institute of Oceanography off the modern temple town of Dwarka and Bet Dwarka uncovered submerged underwater stone masonry, semi-circular bastions, perforated stone anchors, and pottery fragments dating to the late Bronze and early Iron Ages.
imageCredit: Wikimedia Commons / National Institute of Oceanography

name: Viratanagara (Matsya)
event: The 13th year of exile spent in incognito disguise; cattle raid of Virata and unveiling of the Pandavas
description:
Viratanagara was the ancient capital of the Matsya kingdom, tucked among the protective granite ridges of northeastern Rajasthan. Under the terms of their exile, the Pandavas were obligated to spend their thirteenth year entirely unrecognized; discovery by Kaurava spies would mandate a renewal of twelve more years of banishment.

In Viratanagara, the heroes took humble service in King Virata's palace: Yudhishthira as the king's dice companion Kanka, Bhima as the royal master chef Vallabha, Arjuna as the eunuch dance teacher Brihannala, Nakula as master of horses, Sahadeva as cowherd, and Draupadi as queen Sudeshna's maid Sairandhri. After Bhima secretly slew the tyrannical general Kichaka for molesting Draupadi, the Kaurava army attacked Matsya to seize its royal cattle herds. Arjuna, taking Prince Uttara as his charioteer, engaged the entire Kaurava host at the city's borders, routing them single-handedly just as the thirteenth year elapsed.

Modern Bairat is an exceptional archaeological site. In addition to yields of Painted Grey Ware, it houses the Bijak-ki-Pahari hill where two Minor Rock Edicts of Emperor Ashoka were discovered alongside the remnants of a 3rd-century BCE circular Buddhist chaitya temple, confirming its continuous status as a regional capital.
imageCredit: Wikimedia Commons / Archaeological Survey of India

name: Upaplavya
modernLocation: Matsya territory, near modern Viratnagar / Alwar, Rajasthan
event: Allied military encampment of the Pandavas; pre-war diplomacy and peace embassies
description:
Upaplavya was a prominent city or cantonment within the sovereign borders of the Matsya kingdom. Immediately following the public revelation of the Pandavas' true identities and the wedding celebrations of Arjuna's son Abhimanyu to Virata's daughter Uttara, the Pandavas relocated their military headquarters here to organize their response to Kaurava intransigence.

It was in the councils of Upaplavya that kings and confederates gathered from across Bharata, including Krishna, Balarama, Drupada, and rulers of the Chedis and Yadavas. From this city, King Drupada's royal priest was dispatched to Hastinapura to demand the restoration of Indraprastha, and here Dhritarashtra's trusted charioteer-envoy Sanjaya arrived carrying the Kauravas' non-committal messages. When diplomatic pleas faltered, Krishna embarked from Upaplavya on his celebrated final embassy of peace to the royal court of Hastinapura.

Although explicitly attested in the Udyoga Parva as a thriving city close to the Matsya capital, Upaplavya has not been definitively correlated with a specific excavated mound. Scholars place it within the fertile corridor between modern Viratnagar and Alwar in northeastern Rajasthan.

name: Kurukshetra
event: The catastrophic eighteen-day war; discourse of the Bhagavad Gita at Jyotisar
description:
Kurukshetra, revered as Dharmakshetra ('the field of righteousness'), was an expansive plain bounded between the holy Saraswati and Drishadvati rivers. Long consecrated by King Kuru's austerities and Vedic rituals, it was chosen as the cosmic arena where eighteen Akshauhinis (armies) gathered to resolve the dynastic conflict.

On this battlefield, as the conches sounded before the opening clash, Arjuna succumbed to moral despair at the prospect of slaying his kinsmen, teachers, and elders. In response, Krishna delivered the sublime discourse of the Bhagavad Gita, unveiling the immortal nature of the Atman, the doctrine of Nishkama Karma (selfless action), and his cosmic Vishvarupa form. Over eighteen days of merciless warfare, ancient heroes—Bhishma on his bed of arrows, Drona felled by grief, Karna trapped by destiny, and Duryodhana slain at Dvaipayana lake—perished, bringing an epoch to its close.

Kurukshetra has been celebrated continuously in Vedic literature (such as the Taittiriya Aranyaka) and Puranic pilgrim itineraries. The region features numerous monumental water reservoirs including Brahma Sarovar, Sannihit Sarovar, and the sacred banyan tree at Jyotisar, alongside excavated PGW mounds that witness early historic habitation.

name: Prabhasa
modernLocation: Prabhas Patan / Somnath, Gir Somnath district, Gujarat
event: Sacred coastal tirtha; internal destruction of the Vrishnis and passing of Krishna
description:
Prabhasa, situated on the southwestern coast of Saurashtra where the Hiran, Kapila, and mythical Saraswati rivers meet the Arabian Sea, was celebrated throughout ancient India as a premier tirtha for purification, astronomy, and liberation.

Thirty-six years following the Kurukshetra war, omens of doom gathered over the Yadava clan. Journeying to Prabhasa on pilgrimage to propitiate the gods, the Vrishni and Andhaka warriors indulged in heavy drinking and revived old rivalries. An argument escalated into violence; plucking the resilient marsh eraka grass that had grown from the powdered cursed iron pestle of Samba, the blades miraculously transformed into iron clubs, and the warriors slaughtered one another in a frenzy of mutual destruction. Nearby in the coastal forest of Bhalka, as Krishna rested in contemplative samadhi under a Pippala tree, the hunter Jara mistook his lotus-marked left foot for a deer and released his mortal arrow.

Modern Prabhas Patan is universally known for the historic Somnath Jyotirlinga temple standing sentinel over the ocean waves. The Triveni Sangam and adjacent Bhalka Tirtha remain living pilgrimage stations with records of worship and renovation extending back to antiquity.
